parakeet: Christians often argue that the resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God. But that claim skips several prior questions that never actually answers. How do we know there is a God at all? How do we know that this God has a son? How do we know resurrection is the sign this God would use to identify that son? And even if a resurrection happened, how would the event interpret itself? The real problem is that Christians move from this happened to therefore Christianity is true without explaining how this is supposed to mean that. The resurrection does not prove the framework. It depends on the framework already being assumed. Simply put, the resurrection does not prove God, it assumes God. The core issue is not just whether the resurrection happened. It is whether the resurrection, even if granted for the sake of argument, actually proves what Christians say it proves. That's a different question altogether. Because a person can set aside for the moment the historical debate over whether Jesus rose and still ask whether the theological conclusion is logically warranted. In other words, even if we granted the claim, would it actually establish that God exists, that Jesus is God's son, and that Christianity is true? That's where the argument starts to break down. Because Christians often move from something unusual happened to Jesus to therefore God exists, Jesus is divine, and Christian theology is confirmed as if those conclusions naturally follow from the event itself. But they don't. That move skips multiple layers of reasoning and treats them as though they are already settled. It turns a dramatic claim into a complete worldview without explaining how the one is supposed to prove the other. The resurrection argument often presents itself as though it's answering the big questions, when in reality it's quietly assuming them. It does not first establish that a God exists. It does not establish that this God acts in history and recognizable ways. It does not establish that this God has a son or that resurrection is the sign this God would use to identify that son. It also does not independently establish that the gospel reports are reliable enough to support all of that theological weight. Those are not small details. Those are the very premises the conclusion depends on. Instead, the Christian framework is often smuggled in ahead of time, and then the resurrection is treated as if it confirms what was already assumed. That's why the argument feels circular. The resurrection does not solve the God question. It depends on the God question already being answered in a specifically Christian way. So rather than functioning as proof, it functions more like a confirmation story for people who already accept the larger framework. That is the heart of the reasoning problem.
